utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And good morning, Major Jennings.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've been through my notes. I think that we can finish up your cross-examination in 10 or 15 minutes. Let's start by just cleaning up a few loose ends that were left over from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have previously distributed, Your Honour, to counsel for the Prosecution and our co-defendants, a few short exhibits that we intend to use today. The first one is the -- I'm sorry, actually the registrar has the packets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document I would like you to review, Major, is milinfosum number 98. That is dated the 6th of February, 1993, previously marked as Exhibit D49/1.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two points regarding this milinfosum, sir. The first is, it's true that actually both the ABiH and the HVO forces were digging entrenchments, fortified positions, defensive positions; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case. It wasn't just the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And second, there is no mention in this milinfosum of the meeting that you had with Mr. Kordic on that day, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as you've established in other cases, there isn't a record, although I do have my own notes recording the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there are other documents which record such meetings or events which took place, specifically the 1 Cheshire war diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure that's the case. We have not had the opportunity to review that. The next document I would like you to review, sir, is milinfosum 99, from the next day, February the 7th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This does need an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D111/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two very brief points with respect to this document. The first page and a half, essentially, chronicles a list of complaints related to the BritBat representatives by the commander of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, and the comment on page 2 essentially concludes with the observation that these sorts of accusations are being made by both sides. That was consistent with your experience; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is no reference in this milinfosum to your meeting on February the 7th, 1993, with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't. I have this from yesterday. We actually established this point yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I have now two copies of this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The next document I would like to review with you is milinfosum number 103, which has previously been marked as D109/1, 11th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just take a look on the first page of this document. There is a reference to your meeting. The OC of C Company visited the HVO HQ in Busovaca and spoke to the HDZ representative, Dario Kordic. It relates the details of your conversation. It relates accurately the details of the conversation that you had with Mr. Kordic, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instance where, because I was able to get back in time and actually speak, I can recall, to Sergeant Connelly, he had time to actually get it in the milinfosum. As I explained yesterday, this wasn't always the case. It depended on when the information came in. And I see that it does actually, within the milinfo, refer to the HDZ representative, Dario Kordic, when we had the discussion yesterday about the HZ-HD [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can move on. I would just like to show you the milinfosum for February 12th of 1993, milinfosum number 104.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D112/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one point with this, Major, and that is that there is no reference in this milinfosum to the mine-clearing or mine incident that you related in your testimony in chief; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The next document is the next milinfosum, for the following day, February the 13th, 1993, milinfosum number 105.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D113/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it suggested, because there is no mention in the milinfosum, that these incidents didn't occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't believe that that's suggested at all, Your Honour. The only point that I'm making is that these conversations were not deemed sufficiently important to be included in the milinfosums. That's all. I'm not in any way, and I hope the Court doesn't suggest in any way -- or doesn't perceive in any way that I am suggesting that we are attacking the major's veracity. We are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought that wasn't the case, but I just wanted to be sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, milinfosum number 105, major, once again, doesn't contain any reference to the mine-clearing incident, does it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which mine-clearing incident are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident that you referred to where you saw a substantial quantity of explosives --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. So -- so it doesn't contain reference to the fact that I discovered a quantity of mines under a bridge. There was no clearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very -- I stand duly corrected. There is a reference to shelling in the Busovaca area. You can see that on the bottom of the first page, where it is suggested that Bosnian artillery or Bosnian army fire was falling onto HVO positions. Did you ever see any of that when you were present in the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of this specific reported instance, I cannot recall that I would have seen shelling on that day. However, during the period, really, from the start of the conflict up to the day -- that is the 25th of January, when we established a U.N. control point on the bridge at Kacuni, thereafter there was shelling all the time. You would be driving along roads in the course of your duties, and you would hear an explosion, you would record it, and you would report it as such. So this may have taken place whilst I was driving around. It may not have. The fact that it's in the milinfo, as I stated yesterday, I don't discount the validity of it. I would just say that the comment does underline, possibly, Bosnian army fire. I'm sure that they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, I'm not suggesting one thing or another. You were performing your duties under difficult circumstances, and isn't it true that shelling from both sides was actually a regular occurrence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't rule out the fact that the army BiH may have had artillery fire which they used. What I've always stated is I didn't see any myself in my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document brings us to where we finished up yesterday, your conversation on the 23rd of February, 1993, and I would just like the usher to show you milinfosum 116, dated the 23rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D114/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three points with respect to this milinfosum, Major. The first is, as you can see under the Busovaca section, there is no reference to the conversation that you had with Mr. Kordic on that day?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to the conversation I had with Mr. Kordic on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the Vitez section, there's a description of the incident that you described yesterday, during which a Dutch Bat captain, Captain Linsen's Mercedes was apparently hijacked by two individuals while travelling in the Vitez area? The third point that I would like -- you have to say "Yes".

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, an incident which I recall clearly. We were all briefed on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third point I would like to make is on page 2, right before the Gornji Vakuf entry, where it says the CO of the 1st Cheshires and the Vitez-Travnik LO visited the HVO Vitez to request the return of the vehicle and its contents. Were you aware that Colonel Stewart and, I take it, Captain Forgrave had --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Martyn Forgrave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. They had visited the headquarters of the HVO military forces in Vitez to bring this incident to the attention --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I would have been aware of that, and as I said yesterday, the commanding officer had made it clear to us all it was a very high priority. I wouldn't be surprised that a dozen or so officers in various capacities were doing what they could to try and retrieve it, myself included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And finally with respect to the meeting that you had on the 27th of February, this is actually recorded, I think, in milinfosum number 120, dated February 28th, 1993, and I would just like the usher to show you that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D115/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The particular provision appears, Your Honour and Major, on page 2 under the Busovaca entry.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a factual statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You previously described that the chief of police in Vitez actually was the gentleman who arranged for the retrieval of this Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that it was Mr. Pasko by Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasko told you that he had, in fact, arranged that, I take it, when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting with Mr. Pasko was very brief. As I think I've already outlined yesterday, I basically bumped into a stand-off position between two opposing factions, shall we say loosely, HVO, and, well, that's really all that concerned me at the time, that they were opposing factions. Mr. Pasko, shall we say, was rather busy at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Major. I think that's a very understated way of putting it. The last question I have for you is this one, Major: Do I understand that the first time that you met Major Kordic was February 3rd was after the fighting generally had ended and after the negotiated ceasefire agreement was already in place?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the fighting had ended. I don't believe, actually, during the period in question right up to the last meeting I had with Mr. Kordic, that the fighting ever ended. In fact, there was several ceasefire agreements that were made over the period. I couldn't date them, specify them, other than on recollection there were many, and they were broken by both sides. So, no, it wasn't when the fighting had ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much indeed, Major. I appreciate your testimony. That concludes my questioning, unless the Court has any questions for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do I take it from your examination, Mr. Sayers, that there's no dispute about the conversations which this witness had with Mr. Kordic? Mr. Kordic said on one occasion he would hold up the prisoner exchange until various points were sorted out?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That point, Your Honour, is actually disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. On another occasion, he said that, on the question of aid, that they were discussing blocking the road with civilians. Is that disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that point is disputed. But we do not dispute the fact that the Major had the conversations which he has described with Mr. Kordic, or at least that various conversations occurred at the time that he describes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or that the car had been returned thanks to Mr. Pasko?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That point is not disputed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that you'll need to refer to your notes for the questions I have to ask, and these were, of course, extracted from a pocketbook which contains other notes as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a number of topics to deal with, but all quite shortly. First, I think, can I deal with Donja Polje. In respect to that, some statistics from a census were put to you. I would be grateful for sight, if it's possible, of the census statistics that the Defence were speaking from. While that's being considered, can you check or tell us whether you had any entries in any of your pocketbook, other than the ones you've already shown us, that relate to Donja Polje, that is, that relate to what you saw at Donja Polje, not the occasion when there was a reference by Kordic, Mr. Kordic, to Donja Polje?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can say this: I did check my notebooks, I had two, and I believe there are no other references which are relevant to what's happened in the last couple of days, and certainly there's no specific reference to the incident which I did witness, the incident being the observation of one or two HVO soldiers entering a building, which identified to be Muslim in architecture, and then leaving. I believe, from my memory, that it was Donjavic Polje or the area of Donjavic Polje. There were, actually, buildings all the way down from Donjavic Polje to the bridge itself. There was no specific demarcation line. There must have been, obviously, on a map which showed a village boundary, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely. Could you take this map and lay it on the ELMO? And we'll look at the bit that shows Donja Polje. The area that you're speaking of, I think you may have to reposition it a bit, that would probably be sufficient, if it can be sharpened on the bottom right-hand corner, so much the better, but that may not be possible. Thank you. That's perfect. That shows the point that you've made, because we can actually see what appear to be house markings along the side of the road, can we not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are, therefore, marked housing all the way between Donja Polje and Kacuni; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that you saw this incident, first of all, with the emerging HVO soldiers and the house that then went up in flames. Can you be at all precise about whereabouts that was on that road?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be exactly precise, relating to this map, where I actually saw this incident taking place. When I gave evidence and a witness statement was taken, I focused in on this place, Donjavic Polje as a centre of mass, but the destruction of buildings that I saw occurred all the way along this road, as certainly from, if you look at the map now here, the centre of mass of Donjavic Polje going southeastwards all the way to the U.N. checkpoint shown at Kacuni. It would have been in one of these houses along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, the houses that were then seen by you to have been damaged, were they also lying between Donja Polje and Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, but I must say that in relation to my previous statement, I did say Donjavic Polje as well, because I believed that such houses as I've described being destroyed were in there as well, so it is actually both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the quoted census is available for my consideration. Thank you very much. If the usher could produce it so I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, and I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the usher would just hand it to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The entry for Donja Polje is actually referred to as "Polje" in this census on page 2, for the Prosecution's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll just have a look at that, please. Perhaps that can be demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, look at the first sheet to understand how the columns are to be construed, and it totals, then, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Yugoslavs and then others. If we turn to the second sheet, which is the bear statistic that was read out from you, it comes not from Donja Polje but from Polje, and that statistic would suggest no Muslims for Polje, 5 Serbs, 709 Croats, 8 Yugoslavs, and 7 others. Are you aware, one way or another, of how the registration of "others" was typically -- what that typically represented at the time of the censuses?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any case, seven were others. If we then turn back to the first page to Kacuni, which you can see just halfway down, there the Muslims are 963, 9 Serbs, 207 Croats, 3 Yugoslavs, 11 others. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would appear from that that Kacuni is a majority Muslim area, a place called Polje showing no Muslims but some others, and you're not able to identify for which part of this road and area Polje relates?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has this document got an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It had better have one, I think, now. I don't know how it -- what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it had better be a Defence exhibit, since it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it had better be, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D116/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could you tell us with greater precision what it is exactly you wish to tell the Chamber through your intervention? Apparently there were no Muslims in Polje, according to the census. In Kacuni, you tell us that there was an important majority of Muslims. We are agreed on that. And then what else? Are you making any inferences from these figures? Is that what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, the point was this: The cross-examination on this part of the witness's testimony seemed to be aimed at throwing some doubt on whether what was happening was as described by the witness; namely, first, an attack by the HVO on a Muslim house, and second, the destruction of Muslim houses. Because it was suggested, effectively, that what was being described didn't fit with the census statistics, which would have revealed no Muslim occupation, and therefore no Muslims and no Muslim houses, in the area concerned. As we now see, the cross-examination proceeded on an incomplete and, unfortunately, a misleading picture, first because we don't quite know what Polje is. Second, because Polje, in any event, does contain some unattributed others, but most significantly, because the witness's evidence -- as has always been clear from his witness statement, and as is clear in the summary -- relates to an event that happened between Polje, or Donja Polje, and Kacuni. And the statistical material makes it quite clear that it is probable in the extreme that that road contains Muslim property and that his account therefore -- which, as I understand it, was in some way being challenged -- is likely to be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to ask the major, the witness: These houses that he saw burning, under precisely what circumstances was it in Donja Polje, and on what road?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was on the side of the main road, the only main road between Kacuni and, as is shown on the map, Donjavic Polje, as I'm pointing to now, this particular road. If I understand your question correctly, Your Honour, as I said, I can't say exactly which of the houses it was. I do believe that it was in the area in between. And the circumstances were, in the course of patrolling up and down that road, I did not take my Warrior off it, as a standard procedure, because of the threat of land mines, and we all stayed to the main roads. I therefore observed this from the turret of my Warrior, this specific incident to which I relate. And the rules of engagement at the time did not allow us to intervene in such instances; nor, given the state of ongoing fighting, sporadic as it was, would I have left my Warrior to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That clarifies things a little bit regarding this incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could I ask, Mr. Nice, might there be a village between Polje and Kacuni which is not reflected here and which could be the area in which the major saw the houses burning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, I don't know if you are able to help with the completeness of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, I don't know if you are able to help with the completeness of the map -- [Wrong channel of translation] -- village, His Honour said, between Polje and Kacuni. It may be that His Honour had in mind between Donja Polje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and Kacuni, shown on this map, reflected in the census figures.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can help you there. And going by memory, there was clearly a signpost which showed you were entering the village of Kacuni. I can recall this. It was on the side of the road. It was actually just north of the bridge where we had the U.N. checkpoint. I think I can recall a sign for, as I describe it from the map, Donjavic Polje. I cannot recall a sign on the road of a village or hamlet, or anything with an identifiable name, in between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to complete the answer to His Honour Judge Bennouna's question, the Chamber will recall, I think from Professor Donia's evidence, that Muslims regularly enough registered themselves either as Yugoslavs or as others -- as, indeed, may have done other ethnic groupings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second topic, the holding-up of the exchange of prisoners. Just remind us, is this recorded in terms in your pocketbook?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is detailed in the list of notes which I took at the meeting that I had with Dario Kordic on the 3rd of February, 1993, and it comes after the list of complaints which I took down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just lay it on the ELMO again, so that the Chamber can see it. What you wrote, in terms, was, Major?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote after the list of complaints, "No exchange of prisoners" -- I put the word "until 48 hours," for 48 hours, and I then put the date, the 5th of the 2nd, '93, next to it. That was 48 hours hence from the meeting that I was attending at the time. These are the actual notes that I took as Dario Kordic was speaking, and a page or two later, as I've submitted, I then wrote them up, as it were, in longhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you just take us to that passage again as well.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, at the top, it says, "Summary of points for meeting with Dario Kordic on Wednesday, the 3rd of February." A summary of the complaints, the sticking points, and then, in fact, in paragraph 4 relates to the roadblock, and then paragraph 5, specifically, "Exchange of prisoners is delayed for 48 hours, until sometime on the 5th of February."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your attention has been drawn in cross-examination to the specific terms of the ceasefire agreement, but in your discussions with Mr. Kordic, who raised the question of linking an exchange of prisoners to resolution of these complaints?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Kordic who said, in effect, "Therefore, as a result of this, the exchange of prisoners will be delayed for 48 hours." I did not bring the subject up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding at that time that prisoners were being exchanged or were about to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall from memory that efforts were ongoing to organise an exchange of prisoners, an exchange of civilians, an exchange of hostages. There were various levels of exchange of people who, shall we say, were generally being detained, for whatever reason. I was not actively involved in this because it was being dealt with by those who had signed a ceasefire document on the 30th of January. But in the course of daily briefings and in terms of my discussions with other people at the school in milinfo in the operations room, I was aware that there were efforts to try and exchange some people as soon as possible. I also believe, because this was a very big task, that the efforts were concentrating on trying to get just some exchanged as a demonstration of goodwill, so that this would have been a gradual process. However, I can't say that I knew that prisoners or hostages were going to be exchanged at a specific time at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, as you told us in chief, was there a delay in the exchange of prisoners following on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly a delay. Whether it actually lasted the full 48 hours or not, I don't know. As I put in my notebook, there was no specific time given; that's why I put "until sometime on the 5th of February." But I do know that there was a delay. This from talking to people when I got back to the school and over the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A number -- next topic, briefly, a number of milinfosums have been put to you. Some of them you'd read previously, some of them you had never read?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I had never read. Two examples: I'd never read the milinfosum of the 9th of January that was put to me. I'd left my previous job some 12 hours previously -- I had no leave. I went straight to Bosnia -- I was on a plane to Zagreb when this milinfosum was written. In others, as I've explained, I was often out on the ground for two to three days, actually out on the ground doing nothing other than operations and then sleeping and didn't, in fact, return to the school sometimes. And there are gaps in my notebook where I did not attend the 5.00 conferences because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Various statistics have been spoken of and events have been spoken of that are covered in those milinfosums. I'm not going to take you to any of them in detail, save to draw to your attention that the statistic of the 19th of February drew also attention to the fact that of the Muslim soldiers identified, less than 10 per cent were thought to be armed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have a copy of the --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got quite a lot of milinfosums here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber can see it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which date was it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it's coming. The 19th of February.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have one the 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 19th of February.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the one I've been given is the 20th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's D62/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have mine and for convenience can put mine on the ELMO if necessary. It's been highlighted but perhaps we'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This deals with Jajce, the liaison officers commented that the majority of the soldiers were unarmed. There is no evidence of any heavier equipment. The fact that the majority of these soldiers were unarmed agrees with B Company's reports that less than 10 per cent of the soldiers in Jajce Brigade were armed. Does that accord with your recollection, or did you not know anything of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say it would accord equally with any recollection that I may have had at the time in all the milinfosums that were handed to me by the Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I ask on that or any other document in detail. The statistics that have been drawn to your attention, all, of course, focusing on the Muslims as opposed to the Croats, does that affect at all the overall picture you gave of the comparative state of arms of the parties yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not because the statements which I made yesterday are taken from witness statements I've made, are based on my own recollection as a field commander, and I stress, that is where the majority of my time was spent. It was not spent in analysing documents, giving comparative strengths. It was spent on the road, trying to unblock checkpoints, to get sides to talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Second-to-last topic, I think. The engineers who asked you not to tell Kordic, how many times did you see them? Once, or more than once?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineers in question, over a period from early February, possibly the 5th or 6th of February, I would say I saw them maybe a dozen times over a two-week period. Usually in the vicinity of the checkpoint. It was a U.N. controlled point, similar to the one at Kacuni that was established where the roadblock had been removed. It was a similar principle to establish U.N. control of passage as an arbiter between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reference to Kordic and not to tell him, once or on any more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only on the occasion which I related in my testimony. And it was unsolicited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And their demeanour -- last question on this topic -- at the time they said that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were clearly, in my opinion, they were clearly very concerned that he might know of what they were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last topic -- no, last topic apart from two tiny details. The two HOS individuals you met in Dario Kordic's bunker, you've had one document shown to you from April '93?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm not going to go through the exercise of showing a number of documents which show totally different conclusions; that wouldn't be helpful because the witness won't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just tell us, please, they were introduced to you on what basis, as what sort of person?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection, as I stated at the time, was that they were introduced to me as the commander and deputy commander of the HOS in Zenica, and I'm obviously going by my memory here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion that, far from being HVO, that they were BiH representatives?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other reference to the individuals. In fact, it was, I believe, a courtesy to explain who was in the room, because we immediately got down to specific business that we were relating probably of minor detail. They didn't speak whilst I was in the room, and I was only in there for a few minutes, relating to points with regard to the equal distribution or perceived equal distribution of aid. This was the topic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see those same men on a subsequent occasion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I saw both individuals at the meeting which was called by Mr. de la Mota at the UNHCR depot in Zenica, which was set for 4.00 p.m. the following day or, sorry, 4.00 p.m. that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, on either occasion were these people introduced as BiH representatives?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If there had been BiH representatives in Dario Kordic's bunker, would that have been a matter to note and recall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have certainly taken note if that had become clear to me. [Technical difficulties with realtime transcription]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transcript has got a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. It's up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the second meeting, if people there had been introduced as representing in any sense the BiH, would that have been noted?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have noted that. However, I was very much an observer at this meeting. At the initiative of Mr. de la Mota, the issue was very much out of my hands. All I had done was to bring it actually to Mr. de la Mota's attention. After Dario Kordic had made the complaint about the unequal distribution of aid, I spoke to nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've described the bunker as effectively an operations room, with maps and so on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first went in and on subsequent occasions, except for the 27th of February, when it did look like, I would say, an office --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from my experience and also from visiting other headquarters, it looked to me like an operations room from where operations were planned and conducted and orders given out to the ground. That's the impression which I gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any other experience -- any experience, to your knowledge, of seeing Mr. Kordic allow BiH people into this room?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it was suggested -- two tiny details. It was suggested to you that the Vance-Owen Plan was signed on all three sides at one stage in your questioning. Do you know, one way or another, whether it ever was? Just "Yes" or "No" will do.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was put to you that the receipt document for the Mercedes, Exhibit 502, was signed by Mr. Kordic in his role as vice-president of HZ-HB. Would you look at the document? Are you aware that he also signed as "Pukovnik", which is translated as "Colonel"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked then, and my last question just this, about your career, and the point was made -- I'm not sure why -- you've been a major since 1990. There's very few people in the public gallery. Is it right that there may be further gazettings in your career in the near future, just "Yes" or "No"? If you think it's tempting providence, I will not even press the question for an answer.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP JENNINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. That's concludes all I wish to ask the witness, in order not to tempt providence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have the point. Major, thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. That concludes it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness can come in. He's Mr. Weckesser. He's a German national. He, I think, speaks perfectly good English, at a sufficient level to make the need for an interpreter from German into English probably unnecessary. But I think we have an interpreter here, should one be required. The Chamber may recall that as a result of timetable changes of the Chamber and personal difficulties of one of the witnesses we originally intended for this week, there had to be a reordering of witnesses, and Mr. Weckesser was brought up as a person who was available and cooperative enough to come. To some degree, his evidence is out of order, but I don't think it's going to take very long to give, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately I'm not in a position to be able to relate to the Court which items can be led and which can't, because we've just received the proposed outline. But one thing I can tell the Court is that apparently this witness's testimony does not concern our co-defendant, and therefore our co-defendant has informed us that there will be no questions from Mr. Cerkez, and I will be conducting the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As, I think, time is likely to be taken by reorganising the room to accommodate the interpreter, if I'm right, it may be sufficient simply for the interpreter to be kept in reserve, and it may not be necessary to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's see how we get on without the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber may find it helpful, if it still finds the coloured map useful -- I'm going to refer to it -- to turn to the Vares sector north and east of the general area of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Weckesser.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My copy of the map that I've referred to is highlighted in two colours as to certain locations but is otherwise unmarked. I imagine it would probably be quite helpful to simply lay that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: My name is Rolf Weckesser.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you spend some 36 years in the German Air Force, leaving with the rank of colonel, and then being deployed, in May 1993, as part of the ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between October and December, were you a team leader based in Travnik, with an area that included Vares in the east and Maglaj in the northwest, and thus also included Zepce, Kakanj, Breza, and Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On arrival to this mission, were you briefed by Sir Martin Garrod as to who was or were the leading figures in the territory?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely, for both politics and military purposes, who were the leaders?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What names were given to you?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The names were, beside the other vital persons, were Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic as the responsible personnel on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you have before you some records to which you are able to refer for dates and so on. When were those records made in relation to the dated entries that you may find yourself referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, could we be informed of what the witness is referring to? We don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What were the nature of the notes? Perhaps we can find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a question to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood that. I have some -- taken during my stay in Central Bosnia, done personal notes, I have done daily records which went into a record of the RC Zenica as a daily record and was published up to the staff in Zagreb. These are basically the -- because I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just as a matter of principle, Mr. President, I must vigorously object to witnesses called by the Prosecution testifying using notes that have not been previously provided to the Defence. I think we've raised this issue several times before, and I think the time has come where we just have to register the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You registered the objection. Your right is to have the notes when the witness refers to them. If they can be provided before, that's a matter of convenience and obviously it's more satisfactory, but the witness is entitled to refer to the notes while giving evidence and then you are entitled to have a look at them. That's when your entitlement occurs, not before. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, I think you also have -- maybe there will be objection to this, but you also have on the desk, I don't know whether you're looking at it, the summary that's been made of your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vares is where we're going to focus our attention. Looking at the map and using the pointer that you can see to your right-hand side and which you can use to point to things on the map, can you just paint the historical position, in a couple of sentences, of Vares; who occupied it and so on?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Maybe "occupation" is the wrong word. Out of my memory, Vares was a pocket, an HVO pocket, isolated, boundering [sic] in the north to the 2nd BiH Corps and to the south to the 3rd BiH Corps and to the east to the BSA. The area was militarily governed by the Bobovac Brigade. The headquarters was located, I think, about three kilometres due north of Vares on the way -- on the road to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time with which we are concerned, which is October 1993, was there something described as an exile government of Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true that there was an exile government which was located in the south, close to -- in the south of Vares, close to the town of Breza.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These people, or if it was more than one person, had they formerly lived in Vares itself?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That's what I don't know. I can't remember. I only know that the lady, Mrs. Mervana -- and she has a complicated name I can't really pronounce -- she indicated that she has been the elected president of Vares, and she was indicating, in all talks we had, that she will go back to Vares as the president of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this same time, was pressure on the HVO in Vares constant or was it getting stronger?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I arrived in the area I'd say the 5th of October, I remember, and from the early beginning of my working period there the pressure on the HVO was rising. We had records, we had movements, we had reports that the 2nd Corps from the north was moving south, the 3rd Corps was moving northeast from Kakanj area, and in all meetings I had with HVO authorities in the town and in the Bobovac Brigade up to the date of about the 23rd, there was a rising tense atmosphere. At that time, it was really culminating in the transfer or in the cooperation and coordination of a convoy called Joy 2 from Split up to Tuzla. This convoy was hampered several times by the conflicting parties on its way to Tuzla, and the latest it was hampered by the denial of -- initial denial of Vares authorities and to get the Convoy Joy 2 through, mainly because the valley north of Vares -- this must have been the 18th/19th of October -- was blocked by hundreds of Croatian refugees who were coming -- who were supposed to come out of the northwest of Central Bosnia and were intended to be brought to the south, to the Herzegovina area. I had serious, very difficult discussions with the security officer in Vares, Mr. Zvonko Duznejevic, and finally he gave up persistence and he let the Convoy Joy 2 pass. After in the night action, the HVO had taken away the Croats out of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to the detail of what happened at Stupni Do, can you tell us how the rising pressure on the HVO in Vares was finally resolved? Did they eventually give up Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It's an assumption on my side. I mean that I think the HVO in Vares was, from the beginning, let's say the date 20th of October, preparing their retreat. I think it has become obvious to them that they would not be strong enough, by men and by armament, to stand a possible offensive from the Bosnian from the north and from the south, and obviously the BSA had not given the assistance which had been possibly wanted by the HVO. I think this was part of the nervousity [sic] at that time in that area, that the retreat was imminent, and I think all the responsible people in that area knew about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The BSA, I take it, is a reference to the Bosnian Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, the Bosnian Serb army located due east of this area. If I may add this, there were rumours at that time, when talking to HVO officials -- I cannot refer exactly who really stated, but it was stated several times -- that when we questioned the situation of the HVO, that they tried to convince us that they would have tanks available. And when asked where, they pointed to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did the retreat eventually happen?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The retreat, I think it started about the 30th of October, when there was some shooting around the Bobovac Brigade, and the 31st, when I met the new commander, Kresimir Bozic, at his headquarters, when he was begging me to remember is the date of his command -- taking his command. And at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off there, because having painted the overall picture of the tension and the retreat, we'll now go through the matters on which you can help us in chronological order. Did the woman with the unpronounceable name who was the president of the exile government provide intelligence about an alleged attack on the village of Stupni Do, and if so, when did she do that?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the night from the 23rd to the 24th of October, at about 23.00, at the headquarters of the ECMM at Zenica. We got a telephone call from this location close to Breza, I think between Breza and Dabravine, asking for help -- for immediate help for a possible fight or massacre in Stupni Do. At that night, because we were not allowed and supposed to go out and drive at night, I could not do anything, so I had to wait for the next day, for the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th, did you attempt to get to Stupni Do, what could you see, and tell us why, if it was the case, you couldn't enter the village?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Early in the morning of the 24th, we intended to go to Stupni Do following these cries for help from the exile government. The situation in Vares was tense. The control posts were tense. We ended up in the access road towards Stupni Do, which is in the south of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the video booth could focus in on the map exactly where the pointer is. Thank you very much. This map is a map, Colonel, with which you're only recently familiar. You've only seen it, I think, this morning.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it, nevertheless, appear to show the roads or the road into Stupni Do accurately?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I think it shows correctly the road at least I know, which is where the pointer is put on now [indicates], which is due south of Vares. I think that was the road which was blocked and which was supposed to be our access road towards Stupni Do, which is at the dam. I think the railway is crossing there, and there's a tunnel over the road, and at that tunnel HVO forces were blocking the road with some trenches, with some mines, and with dozens of soldiers, not allowing us to get in. Then, standing there discussing about entrance, we saw three pickup-type cars and, I think, one Jeep coming out of that tunnel carrying soldiers, shouting, yelling, showing their arms. They stopped for a while. I really don't know why. And so my interpreter had a chance to talk to them, and he relayed later on to me, he said, "Yes --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to this, Your Honour, unless the witness actually heard the soldiers speaking to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, I think before the witness may contribute, if he may, it's clear that this is simply communication via an interpreter, who would be required in any event. The evidence is as good as it can ever be, in terms of proximity, unless you call the interpreter himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness could indicate whether he heard the soldiers talking to the interpreter, or saw it, and how soon afterwards he himself received the information.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm willing to do. I was standing about four metres apart from that grouping. I saw the interpreter talking to these soldiers, and he immediately relayed this wording to me. And the wording were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you do this, there has been an objection, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this evidence. It could scarcely be more contemporaneous, in our view, and therefore has that degree of reliability about it. What weight is to be given to it, of course, finally, will be a matter for us. Yes, Mr. Weckesser, if you would like to tell us what was said.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The soldiers said, "We did not like to do this job, but we had to do it, and we do not like our leaders," which gave us at that time an assumption or a hint that something has happened which was extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on in the chronology of events, what sort of village was Stupni Do and for what was it noted? And in giving that answer, can you, by reference to the map, maybe, point out how near it was to front lines of the various opposing parties?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: As I said, I came in only at the 5th of October in this area. The area was first, before, handled by another monitor, called Hap Stutt, and he told me, when taking over this area, he said Stupni Do is a very nice valley, with charming people. He also told me at that time, giving me a hint that this is possibly a village where some smuggling is done; that at least is a rumour, or was a rumour at that time, reasoning basically on the fact that Stupni Do was really in a kind of central point between the three warring parties. To the east, immediately -- close to the east to Stupni Do was a bordering to the BSA, to the Serb territory. To the north, it was included, actually -- almost included into the HVO pocket, and to the southwest they had good access to the BiH forces. So it was an ideal point, as it looks to me, for transferring weapons, goods, whatever is possible, among the warring parties. And exchanging goods and arms and whatever among the warring parties was not an extraordinary happening in this kind of war. I experienced this at other locations during my two-year stay in ex-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, I must explain that I wait sometimes for the interpreters to catch up.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then decide to seek access by getting permission from the local relevant brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Since --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Since the access was denied by the soldiers at this blockade in the south of Vares, I proceeded that day to the Bobovac Brigade, and there I met the commander, Emil Harah, who refused to grant access to Stupni Do, pretending to me that there was heavy fighting going on and it would be much too dangerous for me and my team to go there, and there would be a lot of mining around that village. So he promised me that it might be possible, on the next day, to get access to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While you were at the brigade headquarters, did you see some other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. There were dozens of soldiers. Some were inside, in the restaurant close to the area where we had the meeting or the get-together with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again I'm going to interrupt you, because there's a small collection of exhibits. I think they've been provided already. They can be distributed, in readiness for production, in bundles. The first one is a photograph. It may be the photograph should just go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: May I use the photograph as reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If you put it on the ELMO, then the public can see it. That's the advantage. Tell us about what we're looking at, and then tell us about the soldiers that you saw.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is the burned-out Bobovac -- former Bobovac headquarter brigade building [indicates]. Between this pole and this wall over there [indicates] was the gate, a primitive gate, control gate, to get access to the Bobovac Brigade. There you were normally standing for a long time until somebody really tried to pick up, and I think they discussed whether they would receive you or not. It happened also that we had been sent away by saying nobody is in and nobody could talk to us. In this area [indicates] left of the headquarters, at that time I saw, I think in this area, there have been two different type of soldiers. One type of soldier looking from experience to be normal HVO soldiers, and there had been another grouping which looked to me different. When we were standing here [indicates] and waiting for access to get to the commander, they were looking from behind the headquarter towards us, going a few steps forwards and then backward, it appeared to me and it appeared to us that they were somewhat kind of hiding. One person here [indicates] in front of us, actually leading us then to the commander, he looked a little bit like that other type of soldiers we saw wearing a bandanna. He also had gloves on his hands, exposing the fingers, leaving the fingers in the open, carrying the trigger -- with the hand constantly on the trigger as if we would consist of a danger to them, which was no danger, out of question. That was about the situation we found when we tried to meet the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that same day, having failed to get permission from the HVO commander, did you go and speak to the BiH commander, Nehru Ganic?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. On our way back, I think it was in the afternoon, 15.00, around, together with Colonel Hendriksen from the NordBat Battalion, we met the OG commander, BiH commander, Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may just add some colour to your evidence if we put the map back on the ELMO and just point out where the Bobovac Brigade headquarters were and where it was that you went to see the BiH commander.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: [indicates]. So the command post, a relatively primitive command post, in a house, was on the road towards Vares at Dabravine, that was the command post for the OG, and there we met the -- took us with Colonel Hendriksen, the commander. He bitterly accused us at that time of doing nothing. He pretended that a massacre had taken place in Stupni Do. He complained bitterly that NordBat had not and was not intervening in the HVO attack, and he stated at that meeting that out of 220 Muslim inhabitants, former inhabitants of Stupni Do, only 21 had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you given intelligence about vehicles seen to have been leaving Stupni Do, and if so, where did the intelligence come from?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The intelligence -- we got some information came from NordBat. We always kept very, very close contact to NordBat, because they were on scene, and we could only come, actually, for hours out of Zenica, if we had been visiting other areas. So NordBat told us that they had observed several HVO trucks coming out in the night, out of this Stupni Do area and out of the Stupni Do road, in the night from the 23rd to the 24th of October. And I assumed that they had been taking away the looted material, I could not assume anything else, which was taken out of this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, that same day, learn that Sir Martin Garrod was intending to hold a meeting with Dario Kordic in his capacity as vice-president of HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason for the meeting being what?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Primarily on the coordination of the giving back of the two helicopters which had been kept back on a medevac -- on a coordinated medevac mission at Medjugorje. This was the prime aim of this meeting, in order to help out in this kind of conflict. In this conflict, I used the chance to ask Mr. Garrod for a favour, and I had asked him in that night, since I was seriously now concerned about the fate of Stupni Do, to ask Mr. Kordic what was going on in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So at this stage, at the time you made the request for the interview to take place, you were still working on rumour and complaint, no one from the ECMM having gone into Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge at that time, had NordBat gone into Stupni Do, or not?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No, they had not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from the HVO soldiers blocking entry of the road, were you aware of anyone else having access to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this a convenient movement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. I'm getting the French coming through my channel, but we'll adjourn for half an hour. No doubt that can be put right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're at paragraph 14. Did you hear back -- just yes or no to this -- from either Sir Martin Garrod or someone else as to the results of the interview that he had with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Would you repeat, please, the last portion of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear the results of the interview that were had with Dario Kordic? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that Martin Garrod will be being called quite soon. The matter is recorded, in any event, in an ECMM report which I might as conveniently produce through this witness, and then the Chamber will know at least what the narrative is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So can I produce the next exhibit, please, 1263,1, which you will find the first document underneath the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the daily report for the 25th of October, but it deals with the matters you've been telling us about. And on the political situation, it deals with HRC visiting Dario Kordic in Busovaca in connection with the helicopters that you've already spoken of. There are other entries, which I'm not going to go into, and then at the bottom of the page, it says that he was questioned about Stupni Do, and it sets out on the following pages what it was said that he had given by way of comment or explanation. Were you aware of that explanation being given at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I was aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And included, as we can see -- well, let me come back to that. Were you satisfied with the explanation, or did you decide to continue your efforts to get into Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Actually we were not satisfied, because the circumstances, the rumours, the information so far gotten by the BiH, the demands, we were not satisfied. We were still trying to get a clear -- a clear picture on the situation. But we trusted in that promise of Mr. Kordic that he will -- that he look into it, and we hoped, but we were not certain, that it would not look that bad as it finally looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 25th, did you try again, through the Bobovac Brigade commander, Emil Harah, in company with William Stutt?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then did you find out that there had been a change of personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was surprising, especially to Mr. Stutt, who knew Mr. Rajic personally. For me, it was the first get-together with Mr. Rajic, and when Mr. Stutt with his team joined my team in the afternoon and we went to the Bobovac Brigade, we were surprised to find two commanders, not only Kresimir Bosic but also Mr. Rajic, who introduced himself, was his name, and took place on the meeting table, and -- should I refer to the meeting itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, go on and tell us -- but tell us first, where was Rajic known to be a commander from?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I was -- this was part of my initial briefing. I still have some personal notes of that, given at the 5th of October by Mr. Beaumont, that Mr. Rajic was an HVO commander in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: So it was surprising that he was now in Bobovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The meeting focused from the beginning on the access possibility to Stupni Do, and it was surprising from the beginning that the expected commander in charge, Mr. Bosic, did not control the meeting. He almost did not take part in the conversation. The talking was almost purely done by Mr. Rajic, in a friendly, almost charming way, but denying any -- denial of any access to Stupni Do at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On what grounds was access denied?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, I think you had to go to Zepce?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some distance away. And in a sense not the topic you're here to help us with, but in a few sentences, because it may be relevant for our considerations, in Zepce, what evidence did you find of co-operation between Croats and Serbs at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Zepce was -- the Zepce authorities pretended and they played towards us that they were besieged not only by the -- or surrounded not only by BiH in the east and in the south, but also in the north, northwest, from the Serbs. I normally -- despite the fact that based on the Brioni agreement, we were promised to have freedom of movement, the freedom of movement for these teams, especially in the particular areas, was quite often limited and not given. So whenever I went to Zepce for the meetings, in order to prepare or to open a humanitarian corridor aiming towards the starving city, Zavidovici, which was isolated at that time and really surrounded, I was very well escorted from the beginning and had, actually, this exception of the meetings with Mr. Lozancic and Ivo Jozinovic, no possibility to move. But on that occasion I used a break to escape from the escort, and I said to my team immediately, "Get to the car. We'll do a little tour around the town." And it was surprising, after a few house blocks, to get into a warehouse of the HVO, where we pretended to try to buy some chocolate, where we saw ECTF food in the original packages, the original pallets, stored, even under the normal plastic cover they were sealed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "ECTF" meaning ... ?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember, actually, what the abbreviation means. It still is just in my mind, ECTF. I think it was the abbreviation for the -- for the aid which was provided to Bosnia at that time from the EC. This was one, and then we continued our drive, in that break period. And after one turn in the north of Zepce, we ran into a Serbian platoon, tank platoon, fully active, with the flags up, racing out, yelling, charming, smiling to us, racing up to the north, towards the area of Maglaj or Zepce or basically BSA-held territory. This was a clear indication that they had excellent relations at that time, and the HVO with the BSA, this was also admitted personally by Mr. Niko Jozinovic to me by indicating that all the wounded people, the wounded HVO soldiers, are being brought to Banja Luka to be cared for, and that he has to pay a lot of money for that. Another indication how they tried to fake their kind of non co-operation with BSA at that time was that I pretended, with a meeting with Mr. Lozancic, who was the president at that time of Zepce, to need a break, and I asked him twice. I think every time -- no, not twice. Every time I asked him, when I was in Zepce and meeting him, to have a walk through his town to look to the damages done by the Bosnian and Serbs. And we had a walk, and during the walk, he always showed me -- the windows were missing. He was asking for alternatives for the windows, the window was coming soon. And whenever we approached a certain corner, he always stopped me by saying, "This is now getting very dangerous. Here the Serbs are shooting into our town. We should not progress." We always returned at the same spot. This was in contrary, actually, to the observations I had made in regard to the tank platoon. And an additional one: On almost every occasion we went into the Zepce pocket, we saw Serbian staff cars standing in front of the staff building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 20. On the 27th of October, did you succeed eventually then in gaining access to Stupni Do, with the assistance of NordBat and despite resistance?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, how was the resistance overborne, overcome?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The location of the resistance was the same as described before, on the south of Vares at this entrance gate to the road up to Stupni Do. The tunnel itself -- or right after the tunnel, the road was blocked with concertina and with three tank mines, the middle tank mine with an antenna on it, and on the right side, on the left side, a normal -- without antenna, a normal tank mine. We had a discussion -- it was one carrier with us from the NordBat Battalion, we were one Jeep -- and they refused in a very clear way, saying, "No way, you cannot get up there." And very bravely, one NordBat soldier, he pushed one HVO soldier to the chest. He was almost falling back. He took himself the mine in the middle, put it aside, shifted the other two mines to the side of the road, gave a sign to the carrier. The carrier went through the concertina, and we right away, after this carrier, followed up to the road to Stupni Do. I do not observe it -- later on I realised -- that I think a TV team, or at least a team of unknown media, was also chasing behind us into Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So was this, so far as you could judge, the first entry into Stupni Do after the massacre that you're now going -- or the massacre, the remnants of which you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was not the first one. It was the first one for ECMM, for an ECMM team. We had learned that in the evening before, the NordBat had gained already access to the Stupni Do area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think in the village you found complete destruction, some houses still smouldering. You found some 20 bodies, most of them burned beyond recognition, the size of the skull of some of them showing that they were children?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I might add that also in the meanwhile an UKLO team, a United Kingdom liaison team, was coming up; a special force, obviously a small grouping -- they just had one car and three persons -- and there was killed people. And together with them, we were investigating the remains, especially from the bodies of the children, having some kind of children's skulls in our hand. It seemed to me at that time, not being an expert of forensic experience, that these human bodies had been burned together with animals, because at the same location we also found sheep heads, burned sheep heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you search for signs of fighting, that is to say, warfare-type fighting?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. This was of prime interest also for my colleague and me, to look for indications of the suspected heavy fighting. I could not detect, in these hours we spent up in Stupni Do, any sign of heavy fighting. I could not see bullet signs in the walls, in the remaining walls. I could not find any fortification, military-oriented fortification. And we were looking on the ground for small-arm shells, and we only found about five small-arm shells right at the vicinity of a house in the middle of the former Stupni Do, where we in the cellar found, I think, three women, three women which had been killed or had been dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we move to the 31st of October when, I think, you met the man Bozic again --

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- who you had last seen playing a subordinate role in the discussion with Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His behaviour, and what did he say?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Maybe I have to jump back just a little bit, sir. I might add on that on that day when ECMM, together with a NordBat carrier, went up to Stupni Do on the 24th, also later on the chief of staff, I think, of the Vitez BritBat unit was coming in, a gentleman, Ramsey, and in an improvised TV or media conference, which was aiming to, I think, one media team and actually almost transmitting into the blind, he was publicly blaming Mr. Kresimir Bozic for this massacre and telling that this will be pursued. When I met Mr. Bozic on the 31st, he was considerably nervous and referring especially to this presentation of the General Ramsey, and he was indicating to me -- "indicating" is not the proper word -- he was begging to remember and to put down in records that he took command of the Bobovac Brigade on the 24th and not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, now to the next paper exhibit which follows in the stack, which should probably just be placed on the ELMO. You can lay it over the map. That's not a problem, I think. It's Z1276.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: What are we looking for now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the next paper exhibit. It's the ECMM daily report for the 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: 31st of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 31st of October. You can see a couple of entries that relate to Stupni Do.
