utterances.text: -- and the status of those statements, it may be that there are other matters which we ought to deal with fairly soon. Again, when you're planning your calling of witnesses, you might like to identify some time for legal argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, I think I said on the earlier occasion this week, the argument about witnesses who are dead or who are unwilling is really a composite argument which breaks into two parts, but it is nevertheless a composite argument, because the underlying principles applicable to one resolution are probably applicable to the other, and therefore it is better for me to know what, if any, unwilling witnesses there are and what categories they fall into, and at that stage to address the argument about both topics comprehensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Provided the matter is in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It certainly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other dates which I can mention are these: that the last day listed is the 10th of December, which is a Friday. We shall not be sitting that morning, so that means that the last day for sitting will, in fact, be the 9th of December. As I think I may have said before, we shall start sittings in the New Year on Monday, the 10th of January. I think that's the date. I haven't got the calendar with me. But my recollection is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's Monday the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have produced a calendar, which should be with the senior legal officer, for the first four months of this year, indicating what days are available for this trial. And the answer is that apart from two weeks or so, we will have the period between the New Year and Easter available for this trial. That, of course, is subject to change. First of all, change necessary because of this case, and then change necessary due to other cases. We shall want, certainly by the 26th of November, to have a good idea as to when the Prosecution are going to close so we can start planning accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think you're going to be disappointed in the forecast that we'll be able to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. As I say, I will ask the senior legal officer to have copies of the calendar available, and perhaps he can make sure they are handed out to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I make two points about the timetable: First, whenever there's a day that's about to be cancelled, it may be that we do get it at the very earliest moment, but the complexities of getting any single witness here, let alone a week's worth of witnesses, are enormous. Ms. Bauer, who happens to be in court, has to deal with this as one of her many tasks, and she informs me that no witness involves less, in simply arrangements, less than a couple of hours, and frequently it's much more than that. So the earliest possible notification of any day that may be cancelled is helpful to us, even if it's a contingent possibility that doesn't come off. The second thing is, where there is a period marked out as a week clear, we obviously make our -- and I'm sure that the Defence does as well -- we make our own domestic arrangements and private arrangements, including vacations, with those weeks in mind, and any sudden introduction of court sittings can be difficult, and to some degree disagreeable, if it means people cancelling their holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It applies, too, to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think that on the whole, those weeks will not be interfered with. You can take that as being so. We have in mind, of course, the necessity of trying to fix dates and making arrangements for alterations known just as soon as possible. It's inconvenient to everybody if they're made at the last minute. The problem here is the knock-on effect from other cases. Anything anybody else would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, may I take just two minutes? There is one thing, and in all honesty, I really do not know how we should go on in this matter, but I thought it would be wise for me to inform the Court about some facts. We had a Witness C here; I believe we cross-examined him on the 20th of April, and we asked him if he had a wartime diary to which he was referring. He testified here that he had turned over this war diary to the archives of the BH army as the property of the army, to which we responded -- that is, Mr. Cerkez's defence sent a letter to the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina asking them to make that diary available to us. There was no answer. Then we urged an answer, and then eventually they did reply. I have the copies of all this correspondence, in Croatian and in English, for all the parties. We were replied that such a document was nonextant. What confuses me is, of course, we realise that we could use subpoena, but we understand that a practical problem might arise. It might take a very long time, and we hardly believe that the outcome would be favourable. However, I should nevertheless like to have it recorded somewhere that what the witness said was one thing and what the government said was another matter. At least we know now that that diary is gone, does not exist. So all these documents, all this correspondence has been translated, and we should simply like it put on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now on record formally. If you wish the Trial Chamber to have the correspondence, then perhaps you should file it in the normal way, as a notification of the correspondence, and then it will be on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Thank you very much for this advice. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 3.20 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of November, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
